verdict.rationale: Across the Law, Prophets, Gospels, Acts, and Epistles the lexical pattern is uniform: the divine command and invitation are addressed to all hearers without an elect-status qualifier in the text. Acts 17:30 has 'commands' (paraggellei) in the present active indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact, in the active voice), with the dative phrase 'to all people everywhere' (tois anthropois pantachou pantas), governing the infinitive 'to repent' (metanoein). 2 Peter 3:9 negates 'willing' (boulomenos) with 'not' (me) and sets up a 'not, but' (me, alla) antithesis pairing 'any' (tinas) with 'all' (pantas) coming 'to repentance' (eis metanoian choresai). Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11 use 'delight, take pleasure' (chaphets) under the interrogative particle 'he' (the Hebrew question marker) and the oath formula 'as I live' (chai ani) to deny any divine pleasure in the death of the wicked. Isaiah 55:1 issues 'Ho!' (hoy, an attention-calling interjection) plus the plural imperatives 'come' (leku) and 'buy' (shibru) to 'every thirsty one' (kol tsame), with no condition of prior status. The reciprocal duty to preach is equally explicit (Matthew 28:19 'all the nations' (panta ta ethne), Mark 16:15 'to every creature' (pase te ktisei), Romans 10:14-15 the chain of how-can-they-believe questions, 1 Corinthians 9:16 'woe is me if I do not preach the gospel' (ouai gar moi estin ean me euaggelizomai)). The proposition stands and hyper-Calvinism's denial of the free offer and of the duty to evangelize is lexically foreclosed.

scripture.reasoning: The main verb 'commands' (paraggellei, G3853) is present active indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact, in the active voice), meaning God commands, and its dative object is universal: 'to all people everywhere' (tois anthropois pantachou pantas). The infinitive 'to repent' (metanoein) is the content of the command. The triplet 'everywhere' (pantachou) plus 'all' (pantas) plus 'people' (anthropois) piles up universal-scope words around the verb. There is no lexical restriction of the command to the elect; the grammar places the duty to repent on every hearer.

The participle 'willing' or 'purposing' (boulomenos, G1014) is negated by 'not' (me, G3361) and set in a 'not, but' (me, alla) antithesis: not willing 'any' (tinas, G5100) to perish (apolesthai) but 'all' (pantas, G3956) to come 'to repentance' (eis metanoian choresai). The lexical contrast pairs 'any' (tinas) with 'all' (pantas) inside one clause, framing the divine disposition toward the perishing as one of 'patience' (makrothumia) and a wish for their repentance. The verb 'to will' (boulomai) across its 37 New Testament occurrences uniformly denotes purpose or wish, never decree alone.

The aorist (a completed past action) 'I willed' (ethelesa, G2309) with 'how often' (posakis, G4212) expresses a repeated divine wish to gather, 'to gather together' (episynagagein, G1996), like a hen gathering her chicks (simile). It is set against 'you were not willing' (ouk ethelesate). The same root 'to will' (thelo) is predicated of both Christ and the city, and the contrast falls between his willing to gather and their refusal, locating the obstacle in human unwillingness rather than a withheld offer. 'To gather together' (episynago, G1996) occurs only 8 times in the canon, and here governs the children of Jerusalem broadly, not a filtered subset.

The Eindhoven syntactic database (ETCBC) tags this as a question clause (NQ, Ques) using an emphatic infinitive-absolute (Hebrew construction that intensifies the verb) plus finite form of 'to delight or take pleasure' (chaphets, H2654A) with the interrogative particle 'he' (the Hebrew question marker) and negative 'not' (lo): do I at all delight in the 'death' (mut, H4194) of the wicked, and not rather that he 'turn' (shub, H7725) from his ways and 'live' (chayah, H2421). The rhetorical question expects a negative answer, asserting that God takes no pleasure in the wicked dying and desires his turning and living. 'To delight' (chaphets, H2654A) occurs 63 times in the canon and consistently denotes positive desire or pleasure of the will.

The verse opens with the divine self-oath 'as I live' (chai ani, H2416A), the strongest asseverative (solemn-affirmation) formula in Hebrew prophecy. The verb 'to delight' (chaphets) is then negated ('if I take pleasure in the death of the wicked' (im echpots bemot harasha)), and the alternative is 'but rather that the wicked turn from his way and live' (ki im beshub rasha midarko vechayah). The same lemma pair 'to delight' (chaphets) plus 'to turn' (shub) plus 'death' (mut) appears as in Ezekiel 18:23, here intensified by an oath and capped with the double imperative 'turn, turn' (shubu, shubu). This is a pan-prophetic (spread across the whole body of prophetic writings) anchor that the divine pleasure does not lie in the death of the wicked.

The verse opens with the attention-calling interjection 'Ho!' (hoy, H1945) plus 'every thirsty one' (kol tsame), and a chain of plural imperatives 'come' (leku, H3212), 'buy' (shibru, H7666), and 'eat' (ekolu), repeated for emphasis. The invitation is offered 'without money and without price' (belo kesef ubelo mechir), to all who thirst. The lexical scope is unrestricted by the words themselves: the call goes out to anyone in need with no condition of prior status. The Eindhoven syntactic database (ETCBC) marks the clause as a quotation (Q) with interjection (Intj) and vocative (Voct, direct-address) functions, confirming a direct universal address.

The canon's closing invitation stacks three present imperatives 'come' (erchou, G2064) and one aorist imperative (a completed past-form command) 'let him take' (labeto, G2983) governed by an open relative 'the one willing' (ho thelon, G2309). The scope is set by the substantive participle 'the one thirsting' (ho dipson) and the adverb 'freely, without cost' (dorean, G1432). The vocabulary is the lexical mirror of Isaiah 55:1 (universal-call vocabulary closing the canon), and the conditioning clause is 'the one willing' (ho thelon), not the one elect.

The plural imperative-adverb 'come hither' (deute, G1205) governs 'all' (pantes, G3956) 'who labor and are heavy laden' (hoi kopiontes kai pephortismenoi), with 'to me' (pros eme) placing the destination on Christ. The vocative scope (direct-address reach) is set by 'all' (pantes) plus participial substantives describing condition, not status. 'Come hither' (deute, G1205) occurs only 12 times in the canon and is uniformly a wide-open summons.

The aorist participle (completed-action participle) 'going' (poreuthentes, G4198) governs the aorist imperative 'make disciples' (matheteusate, G3100) with object 'all the nations' (panta ta ethne). The combination 'all' (panta) plus 'nations' (ethne) (G3956 plus G1484) defines the scope of the disciple-making duty as unrestricted. Hyper-Calvinism's denial of evangelistic duty cannot be sustained against this imperative with its universal scope.

The aorist imperative 'preach' (kerukate, G2784) takes the dative phrase 'to every creature' (pase te ktisei, G3956 plus G2937) as the audience of the 'good news' (euaggelion). The dative of audience is unrestricted; the noun 'creation, creature' (ktisis) here functions as a comprehensive scope marker. The duty to preach is universal-scope by the words of the command itself.

A rhetorical chain of 'how' (pos, G4459) interrogatives: how can they 'believe' (pisteuo, G4100), how can they 'hear' (akouo, G0191), how can someone 'preach' (kerusso, G2784) unless 'sent' (apostello, G0649). The grammar presupposes that preaching is the necessary instrument of believing for any hearer; if the gospel were not for all to hear, the chain of questions would lose force.

Paul places himself under 'necessity' (ananke, G0318) of 'preaching the gospel' (euaggelizesthai, G2097), and pronounces 'woe' (ouai, G3759) on himself if he does not preach the gospel. The lexical pairing of 'woe' (ouai) with not-preaching makes the proclamation duty inescapable for the apostle; by extension the canon does not treat preaching as optional in light of God's decree.

'No one is able to come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him' (oudeis dunatai elthein pros eme ean me ho pater ho pempsas me helkuse auton). The verb 'to draw' (helkuo, G1670) and the negated 'is able' (dunatai, G1410) state the Godward dependence of coming. This is the strongest pro-hyper-Calvinist text in scope, but it speaks to the cause of coming, not the scope of the call. It limits ability, not the addressed audience. It coexists in the same Gospel with John 7:37 'if anyone thirsts, let him come to me' (ean tis dipsa erchestho pros me), addressed to 'anyone' (tis, G5100). The two together yield divine drawing as the cause and universal call as the published instrument.

complicating_texts.resolution: The verb 'to delight' (chaphets) here can be read as covenantal or preceptive (revealed-command) will rather than decretal (eternal-decree) will, which on a hyper-Calvinist account might soften its force as a universal free offer. The lexical data favor the stem: the form is an emphatic interrogative expecting the answer no, the parallel Ezekiel 33:11 reinforces the same disposition with the 'as I live' (chai ani) divine oath, and the cross-reference chain to Ezekiel 18:32 keeps the same 'to delight' (chaphets) plus 'to turn' (shub) plus 'to live' (chayah) pattern. The text states a divine disposition without ranking decretal versus preceptive categories; the stem affirms a universal free offer, which the words sustain on any reading.

The antecedent of 'you' (humas) and the referent of 'any' (tinas) plus 'all' (pantas) can be narrowed to the covenant community rather than all humanity. Even on that narrower reading, the lexical antithesis 'not' (me), 'any' (tinas), 'but' (alla), 'all' (pantas) still establishes that the divine 'willing' (boulomai) moves toward repentance and away from perishing for every member of the addressed group. Hyper-Calvinism's denial of a free offer cannot lean on this verse because the disposition itself is not narrowed by the words to any subset within the addressed group.

The hyper-Calvinist reading uses 'no one is able to come unless the Father draws him' (oudeis dunatai elthein ean me ho pater helkuse) to argue that the gospel call is in effect only to the drawn. The lexical scope of John 6:44 is causal (no one is able to come unless), not vocative (direct-address); it speaks to the source of effectual coming, not the breadth of the published call. In the same Gospel John 7:37 issues 'if anyone thirsts, let him come to me' (ean tis dipsa erchestho pros me), addressed to 'anyone' (tis) without elect filter. The two verses together yield divine drawing as cause and universal call as publication. They do not cancel one another; they describe two distinct lexical functions.

'As many as had been appointed to eternal life believed' (hosoi esan tetagmenoi eis zoen aionion episteusan) uses 'to appoint, order' (tasso, G5021) of a divine ordering of the believers. The verb describes who in fact believed, not who was addressed. Acts 13 has already shown Paul addressing the synagogue and Gentiles together (Acts 13:26, 13:46) with a universal-scope appeal, so the appointment language in verse 48 concerns outcome, not the breadth of the offer.

variant_units_examined.note: The Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament (SBLGNT) sigla mark a textual choice between 'Lord' (kurios) and other readings for the subject of 'delays' (bradunei) and 'willing' (boulomenos), but the universal-scope phrase 'all to repentance' (pantas eis metanoian) is stable across all witnesses.

The addressee pronoun varies ('you' (humas) versus 'us' (hemas) in some witnesses). This affects the narrower scope of the addressee group but does not touch the 'not, any, but, all' (me, tinas, alla, pantas) antithesis itself, so the disposition-toward-repentance reading holds.

Minor Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament (SBLGNT) marker on placement of 'commands' (paraggellei) and on the spelling of 'everywhere' (pantachou); none of the universal-scope words is in variant dispute.

variants.note: All New Testament anchors are outside the ingested Editio Critica Maior (ECM, the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) 3 John window. Inspected Society of Biblical Literature Greek New Testament (SBLGNT) and Nestle-Aland 28th edition (NA28)-aligned apparatus markers carry minor variants on word order and pronoun choice, none of which touch the universal-scope vocabulary ('all' (pantas), 'everywhere' (pantachou), 'people' (anthropois), 'to every creature' (pase te ktisei), 'all' (kol), 'Ho!' (hoy), 'come' (leku)). Old Testament anchors (Ezekiel 18:23, Ezekiel 33:11, Isaiah 55:1) are not in ECM scope.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Even when 'to delight' (chaphets) in Ezekiel 18:23 and 33:11 and 'to will' (boulomai) in 2 Peter 3:9 are assigned to revealed or preceptive (revealed-command) will rather than the eternal decree, the lexical fact remains that the command and invitation are addressed to all hearers without an elect filter, which is what the stem asserts.

The imperatives in Isaiah 55:1, Revelation 22:17, Matthew 11:28, Matthew 28:19, and Mark 16:15, together with the present-active 'commands' (paraggellei) in Acts 17:30, all addressed to all and to every creature, read straightforwardly as a free and well-meant offer with the duty to respond placed on every person and the duty to publish placed on the messengers.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: hyper-Calvinist lens (stated in its strongest form)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: The strongest lexical form of the hyper-Calvinist case appeals to John 6:37, John 6:44, John 6:65, Acts 13:48 ('to appoint' (tasso, G5021) of those appointed to eternal life), and Romans 9:18 ('mercy' (eleos) and 'to harden' (skleruno) predicated of God's choice) to argue that the effectual call goes only to the drawn, that the offer cannot be truly well-meant toward the non-elect, and that the duty to evangelize is not universal. Lexically, however, these texts speak to the cause and outcome of believing, not to the scope of the addressed call. They do not negate 'commands all everywhere' (paraggellei pantas pantachou) (Acts 17:30), 'to every creature' (pase te ktisei) (Mark 16:15), 'all the nations' (panta ta ethne) (Matthew 28:19), 'every thirsty one' (kol tsame) (Isaiah 55:1), or 'the one willing' (ho thelon) (Revelation 22:17). The universal-call vocabulary and the universal-preach imperatives sit side by side with the drawing vocabulary; the words do not cancel one another.

hermeneutics.notes: The lexical pattern is read most cleanly as two compatible categories: divine drawing as the cause of effectual coming (John 6:44 'to draw' (helkuo)), and a universal published call plus an unrestricted duty to preach (Acts 17:30 'commands all everywhere' (paraggellei pantas pantachou), Mark 16:15 'to every creature' (pase te ktisei), Matthew 28:19 'all the nations' (panta ta ethne), Revelation 22:17 'the one willing, let him take' (ho thelon labeto)). The verdict turns on the universal scope words 'all' (pas), 'everywhere' (pantachou), 'to every creature' (pase ktisei), 'all the nations' (panta ta ethne), 'all' (kol), 'Ho!' (hoy), and on the imperatives addressed to anyone in need, not on any single soteriological (salvation-doctrine) framework.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Describe the lexical scope of the gospel command, the gospel invitation, and the duty to preach in Acts 17:30, 2 Peter 3:9, Matthew 23:37, Ezekiel 18:23, Ezekiel 33:11, Isaiah 55:1, Revelation 22:17, Matthew 28:19, Mark 16:15, Romans 10:14-15, and 1 Corinthians 9:16: to whom is repentance commanded, to whom is the invitation extended, on whom is the duty to preach laid, and is any condition of prior status placed on the hearer or messenger in the text?
stem_audit.notes: The stem phrase 'well-meant offer' and the framing 'not contingent on the hearer's elect status' import a specific intra-systematic debate vocabulary. The neutralized form strips the systematic label and asks only what the lexical scope of the command, the invitation, and the duty to preach is. The verdict is derived on the original stem: the texts command all to repent, extend the invitation to all who thirst and all who labor, and lay the duty to preach on the messengers without an elect filter on the audience. The obstacle to coming is located in human unwillingness (Matthew 23:37 'you were not willing' (ouk ethelesate)), which affirms the original proposition and denies hyper-Calvinism. VERDICT-CHANGED: no, verdict unchanged from the prior file; enrichment added Ezekiel 33:11, Revelation 22:17, Matthew 11:28, Matthew 28:19, Mark 16:15, Romans 10:14, 1 Corinthians 9:16, and a fair statement of the John 6:44 plus Acts 13:48 plus Romans 9:18 hyper-Calvinist case under competing lenses.

lay_summary: This question asks whether the Bible presents the gospel as freely offered to everyone, with God commanding all people to repent and believe, and with the church bound to publish that call. The original words point clearly in that direction, and the pattern is broad enough to span the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, Acts, the Letters, and the closing chapter of the canon. In Acts 17:30 the verb translated 'commands' (paraggellei) is a present-tense form (ongoing, simple statement of fact), and its reach is spelled out as 'all people everywhere' (pantas anthropois pantachou), using three universal-scope words stacked together. The thing commanded is 'to repent' (metanoein). In 2 Peter 3:9 the writer sets up a sharp contrast: God is not 'willing' (boulomenos) that 'any' (tinas) should perish, but that 'all' (pantas) should come 'to repentance' (eis metanoian). The words any and all sit on opposite sides of a 'not, but' (me, alla) construction, so the stated desire moves toward the repentance of all. In Ezekiel 18:23, and again under a divine oath 'as I live' (chai ani) in Ezekiel 33:11, the Hebrew is built as a pointed question that expects the answer no: God takes no 'pleasure' (chaphets) in the death of the wicked, but desires that he 'turn' (shub) and live. Isaiah 55:1 opens with 'Ho!' (hoy, an attention-call) to 'every thirsty one' (kol tsame), inviting them to come and receive without money and without price, and the canon's closing chapter, Revelation 22:17, echoes the same vocabulary with three imperatives saying 'come' (erchou) and a free invitation to 'the one willing' (ho thelon) to take the water of life 'freely' (dorean). The duty to publish that call is just as plain: the Great Commission addresses 'all the nations' (panta ta ethne), Mark 16:15 says preach to 'every creature' (pase te ktisei), Romans 10:14 strings together how-can-they-believe questions that assume the gospel is for any hearer to hear, and Paul says 'woe' (ouai) to me if I do not preach. The denial of the free offer and of universal preaching cannot be drawn out of these words; the words push the other way. There are texts that speak of divine drawing and divine choice, like John 6:44 ('to draw' (helkuo)) and Acts 13:48 ('appointed' (tasso)), and a fair reading takes both seriously: drawing describes the cause of coming, and the universal call describes how the gospel is published, and the words of one set do not cancel the words of the other.
